checks.do: Which Azure roles the deployment script needs, since the pages word them as both roles and as either role.
That Microsoft.Web and Microsoft.Insights are registered as resource providers in the subscriptions.
That the Entra ID diagnostic settings were configured by hand for user and service principal decoys, since they are not handled via the deployment script.

prerequisites.statement: Azure setup requires a Microsoft Azure account with a valid subscription, an Azure user with Cloud Device Administrator and Global Administrator roles to run the deployment script, the Restrict access to Azure AD administration portal option enabled under User settings (to restrict decoy users from the administrator portal), and Microsoft.Web and Microsoft.Insights registered as resource providers in the subscriptions.

quotes: A Microsoft Azure Account with a valid subscription.
An Azure user with Cloud Device Administrator and Global Administrator roles to run the deployment script.
Enabled the Restrict access to Azure AD administration portal option under User settings. This restricts decoy users from accessing the administrator portal.
Microsoft.Web and Microsoft.Insights are registered under resource providers in your subscriptions.

account-key.statement: Cloud Deception for Azure is set up and managed separately per combination of Tenant ID and Subscription ID, so several accounts can share a Tenant ID with different Subscription IDs.

quotes: You can set up and manage Cloud Deception for Azure separately based on the combination of Tenant ID and Subscription ID. For example, you can add multiple accounts that share the same Tenant ID but have different Subscription IDs.

terraform-package.statement: Azure Terraform-based deployment downloads a ZIP containing azure-decoys.tf.json, the admin adds back-end details to its backend block, and `terraform output -json decoys_output > deployment-output.json` produces the JSON file whose upload updates the status in the Admin Portal.

quotes: A ZIP file containing all necessary files is downloaded to your system.
open the azure-decoys.tf.json file in a text editor.
Locate the backend block in the azure-decoys.tf.json file. Add your back-end details and save the file.
terraform output -json decoys_output > deployment-output.json
Select the downloaded JSON file to update the status to the Deception Admin Portal.

management-resources.statement: The Azure deployment script creates a Management Resource Group (holding the function app, logging storage account, app service plan and other management resources) and a Decoy Resource Group in which all decoys are created, whose prefix string is specified during setup.

quotes: A resource group in which all decoys are created. The prefix string for the Decoy Resource Group is specified while setting up Cloud Deception with Azure.
A resource group in which all necessary management resources such as Function App, Logging Storage Account, App Service Plan, etc. are created to support Cloud Deception functionalities.

log-collection.statement: For Azure decoys the deployment script enables diagnostic settings that push diagnostic logs to a Logging Storage Account, and the Admin Portal polls logs from the logging resources every 3 minutes to generate events.

quotes: The Zscaler Deception Admin Portal polls logs every 3 minutes from the logging resources created by the deployment script to generate events.
The appropriate diagnostic setting is enabled for all decoy resources to push all diagnostic logs to this storage account for analysis and generating alerts on the Deception dashboard.

log-service-principal.statement: The Client ID and Client Secret created by the Azure deployment script are a service principal with access to poll log files from the logging storage account.

quotes: A service principal that has access to polling log files from the created logging storage account.

decoy-access-role.statement: The Decoy Access Role has full access to the Decoy Resource Group and is associated with the user and service principal decoys created in the Admin Portal.

quotes: A role that has full access to the Decoy Resource Group. This role is associated with the user and service principal decoys created in the Deception Admin Portal.

health-check-scope.statement: The Azure Decoy Health Check Function App is triggered every 15 minutes from the Admin Portal to check whether deployed decoys exist in Azure and does not check the actual health of the deployed Azure resources.

quotes: A function app that is triggered at an interval of 15 minutes from the Deception Admin Portal to check whether the deployed decoys exists in the Azure cloud. This function app does not check the actual health of the deployed Azure resources.

workflow-identities.statement: The Azure deployment script creates a user decoy as an Azure AD (Entra ID) user with the Decoy Access Role and diagnostic setting for logging, a service principal decoy (Client ID and Client Secret) with the Decoy Access Role and diagnostic setting, and a managed identity decoy as a user-assigned managed identity with the Decoy Access Role.

quotes: Create an Azure AD (Entra ID) user, associate the Decoy Access Role with it, and enable the diagnostic setting for logging.
Create a service principal (Client ID and Client Secret), associate the Decoy Access Role with it, and enable the diagnostic setting for logging.
Create a user-assigned managed identity and associate the Decoy Access Role with the managed identity.

workflow-resources.statement: The deployment script builds an app service decoy as a web app with a managed identity holding the Contributor and Website Contributor roles, a storage account file share decoy with the TransactionOptimized access tier, and a container registry decoy as an empty container registry.

quotes: Create a web app and create a managed identity for the web app, associate the Contributor and Website Contributor roles to it, and enable the diagnostic setting for logging.
create a file share with the TransactionOptimized access tier, upload the decoy file datasets, and enable the diagnostic setting for logging.
Create an empty container registry and enable the diagnostic setting for logging.

workflow-key-vault-arm.statement: The key vault decoy workflow adds passwords or keys of the created user or service principal decoys as decoy datasets; the ARM template decoy workflow creates a deployment template that deploys no actual resources but creates an entry in the template deployment history.

quotes: Create a key vault, add passwords or keys of the created user or service principal decoys as decoy datasets in the vault, and enable the diagnostic setting for logging.
This template does not deploy any actual resources but creates an entry for template deployment in the history.

vm-image-workflow.statement: For an Azure VM image decoy the script deploys a Standard VM instance to create the snapshot, the instance persists for 5 minutes and is terminated after the snapshot is built, and public VM image decoys also get a shareable link for use as a landmine lure.

quotes: A Standard VM instance is deployed to create the snapshot. The VM instance persists for a duration of 5 minutes and is terminated after the snapshot is built.
For public VM image decoys, a shareable link is also created for adding it as a lure in landmines.

user-decoy.statement: An Azure user decoy is an Azure AD (Entra ID) user used to detect sign-in attempts with its credentials; it has access to all other Azure decoys in the Decoys Resource Group, and the name typically has the form <username>@<domainname> with lure names such as admin, administrator, cloud-admin and db-admin recommended.

quotes: You can create Azure AD (Entra ID) decoy users to detect any attempt to sign in using the credentials of the decoy users.
These decoy users have access to all other Azure decoys that are part of the decoy resource group (Decoys Resource Group) configured by Zscaler Deception.
The typical format is <username>@<domainname>. Zscaler recommends using names that lure adversaries, such as admin, administrator, cloud-admin, db-admin, etc.

entra-diagnostics-manual.statement: For Azure user decoys the Entra ID diagnostic setting selects SignInLogs and NonInteractiveUserSignInLogs and archiving them to the integration's logging storage account; this configuration is not handled via the deployment script, as enabling diagnostic settings via API requires a P1 or P2 subscription.

quotes: select the SignInLogs and NonInteractiveUserSignInLogs checkboxes to configure data sources for sending the logs to the logging storage account created as a part of the integration.
This configuration is not handled via the deployment script, as enabling diagnostic settings via API requires a P1 or P2 subscription.

entra-diagnostics-sp.statement: For Azure service principal decoys the Entra ID diagnostic setting selects ServicePrincipalSignInLogs to send logs to the integration's logging storage account; this configuration is not handled via the deployment script, as enabling diagnostic settings via API requires a P1 or P2 subscription.

quotes: select the ServicePrincipalSignInLogs checkbox to configure a data source for sending the logs to the logging storage account created as a part of the integration.
This configuration is not handled via the deployment script, as enabling diagnostic settings via API requires a P1 or P2 subscription.

service-principal-decoy.statement: A service principal decoy carries credentials, any sign-in attempt with them is detected as an attack or compromise, it has access to all other Azure decoys in the Decoys Resource Group, and a Client ID is associated with it automatically.

quotes: You can create service principal decoys with credentials attached to them. Any attempt to sign in using the credentials of the service principals will be detected as an attack or compromise.
These service principal decoys have access to all other Azure decoys that are part of the decoy resource group (Decoys Resource Group) configured by Zscaler Deception.
In addition, a Client ID is also associated with the service principal automatically.

managed-identity-decoy.statement: A managed identity decoy is a user-defined managed identity with access to all other decoy resources in the Decoys Resource Group; an alert is generated if an adversary uses it to access decoy resources, and Deception does not associate it with any production resources.

quotes: You can create a managed identity decoy (user-defined) that has access to all other decoy resources in a decoy resource group (Decoys Resource Group) configured by Zscaler Deception. If an adversary uses the managed identity to access decoy resources, an alert is generated.
Deception does not associate the managed identity with any production resources.

app-service-attack-paths.statement: The documented attack paths of app service decoys are commands executed via a hosted web shell, commands executed via the Kudu endpoint if misconfigured, and theft of the token of the attached managed identity (which has access to all other decoys in the decoy resource group) for privilege escalation; the URI and Source Control Manager URI are generated after deployment.

quotes: The app service decoys can detect the following attack paths:
Web Shell: You can host a web shell that adversaries use to execute commands. Any command executed via the web shell is detected and logged as an attack.
Kudu Endpoint: Every app service hosts a buddy site or kudu endpoint that can be exploited by adversaries (if misconfigured) to execute commands on the host server hosting the app service.
Managed Identity: A managed identity is attached to the app service that has access to all other decoys in the decoy resource group.
Adversaries can steal the token of this managed identity to attempt privilege escalation. Such attempts are detected and logged as an attack.
In addition, URI and Source Control Manager URI are generated and associated with the app service decoys automatically.

storage-container-decoy.statement: Storage account container decoys detect public-container enumeration by organization keywords and private-container access via compromised identities; the ACL choices are Container (anonymous access to container and blobs), Blob (anonymous access to blobs only) and Private (no anonymous access).

quotes: The storage account container decoys can detect the following attack paths:
Public: Adversaries can enumerate public storage accounts using keywords related to an organization to find exposed storage account containers on the internet in an attempt to steal sensitive data.
Private: Adversaries with compromised identities of your organization can target storage account containers that are accessible via the compromised identities.
Container: Allows anonymous access to the container and blobs.
Blob: Allows anonymous access only to the blobs.
Private: Doesn't allow anonymous access to the container and blobs.

file-share-decoy.statement: A storage account file share decoy is a file share mountable on endpoints over SMB or NFS that holds a decoy file dataset.

quotes: a file share service mountable on endpoints and can be Server Message Block (SMB) protocol or Network File System (NFS) protocol.
Zscaler Deception allows you to create storage account file share decoys that include decoy file datasets and mount them on endpoints to lure adversaries.

key-vault-decoy.statement: A key vault decoy includes credential files with URLs to Threat Intelligence decoys containing random user names and passwords, and acts as a cloud lure.

quotes: You can create a key vault decoy that includes enticing credential files with URLs to the Threat Intelligence (TI) decoys containing random user names and passwords. These decoys act as cloud lures.

arm-template-decoy.statement: ARM template decoys embed lures for user decoys, service principal decoys and Azure IaaS URLs of key vaults and storage account file shares; the documented attack paths are plaintext credentials in template specs and deployment histories; they always fail when deployed and generate no event in Deception.

quotes: You can create ARM template decoys with embedded lures for other Azure identity-based decoys such as user decoys, service principal decoys, and Azure IaaS URLs that belong to key vault and storage account file shares.
The ARM template decoys can detect the following attack paths:
Plaintext Credentials: Adversaries look at ARM template specs for exposed credentials.
Deployment History: Create a failed deployment from this template. Adversaries look at deployment histories to find templates (which might have been deleted) with exposed credentials.
The ARM template decoys do not generate an event in Zscaler Deception.

When deployed, the ARM template decoys always fail. However, if you enable history when configuring ARM template decoys, an adversary can still use the deployment history to fetch information from the failed ARM template deployment.

container-registry-decoy.statement: Azure container registry decoys (public or private) detect image pulls to extract credentials or steal code and image pushes for supply chain persistence, and a URI is generated after deployment.

quotes: Pull: Adversaries look for images in the container registry to access the files to extract credentials or steal application code.
Push: Adversaries can attempt supply chain attacks by pushing a vulnerable image to a container registry for persistence.
In addition, the URI to access the container registry is generated and associated with the decoy automatically.

vm-image-decoy.statement: A VM image decoy snapshot (public or private) creates a VM temporarily, adds a callback script for detection and creates a snapshot; Public makes the image accessible to anyone using the Disk URI while Private limits access to internal adversaries, and the Disk URI is generated after deployment.

quotes: You can create a VM image decoy snapshot (public or private) that creates a VM temporarily in Azure, adds a callback script for detection, and creates a snapshot.

Visibility: Select Public from the drop-down menu if you want the VM image to be accessible to anyone using Disk URI. Otherwise, select Private to limit access to the VM image to internal adversaries.
In addition, the Disk URI is generated and associated with the VM image automatically.

gen-ai-decoy.statement: An Azure Gen AI decoy uses Azure OpenAI models in Azure AI Foundry, the selected model must be available in the selected Azure region, and Azure obfuscates the last octet of the IP addresses of users who interact with Gen AI decoys, and Zscaler recommends avoiding containment of these IP addresses from the Investigate page or through Orchestration rules.

quotes: You can create a Gen AI decoy using Azure OpenAI models in Azure AI Foundry.
Ensure that the OpenAI model you want to deploy is available in the selected Azure region.

Azure obfuscates the last octet of IP addresses of the users that interact with Gen AI decoys. Zscaler recommends avoiding containment of these IP addresses from the Investigate page or through Orchestration rules.

resource-group-region.statement: In the Azure managed identity, app service, storage account container, storage account file share and key vault decoy windows, a new resource group is created in the region selected for the decoy, while with an existing resource group the decoy's region and the group's region can differ.

quotes: If you are creating a new resource group while adding the decoy, the resource group is created in the region selected for the decoy. However, when selecting an existing resource group, the deployment region of the decoy and the resource group can be different.

If you are creating a new resource group while adding the decoy, the resource group is created in the region selected for the decoy. However, when selecting an existing resource group, the deployment region of the decoy and the resource group can be different.

If you are creating a new resource group while adding the decoy, the resource group is created in the region selected for the decoy. However, when selecting an existing resource group, the deployment region of the decoy and the resource group can be different.

If you are creating a new resource group while adding the decoy, the resource group is created in the region selected for the decoy. However, when selecting an existing resource group, the deployment region of the decoy and the resource group can be different.

If you are creating a new resource group while adding the decoy, the resource group is created in the region selected for the decoy. However, when selecting an existing resource group, the deployment region of the decoy and the resource group can be different.

lure-methods-identity.statement: Per the Azure lures page, user decoys are lured by placing their credentials on endpoints via landmine policies using Cloud Lures, Session Lures via Bash History and File Decoys via Credential Files, and service principal decoys can be lured on endpoints using the same three methods; landmine agents create a logged-on session with the user decoy credentials, which reaches other decoy resources such as storage account containers and file shares.

quotes: You can lure attackers using user decoys by placing their credentials on endpoints via landmine policies.
The landmine agents create a logged-on session using the user decoy credentials, which allows users to access other decoy resources such as storage account containers and file shares.
Cloud Lures
Session Lures via Bash History
File Decoys via Credential Files
evidence.after: You can place credentials of user decoys on endpoints by configuring lures using the following methods:

quotes: Cloud Lures
Session Lures via Bash History
File Decoys via Credential Files
evidence.after: In addition, you can configure lures for service principal decoys on endpoints using the following methods:

lure-methods-resources.statement: Per the Azure lures page, app service decoys use Browser Lures and Session Lures; private storage account container decoys use Cloud Lures and Session Lures via Bash History (cloud lures make the container accessible via Azure File Explorer); container registry decoys use browser lures, file decoys and session lures; VM image decoys use browser lures or session lures.

quotes: Browser Lures
Session Lures
evidence.after: You can also configure lure attackers for app service decoys using the following methods:

quotes: Cloud Lures
Session Lures via Bash History
evidence.after: If the storage account container decoy is configured as private, then you need to set up lures using the following methods:

quotes: When configured using cloud lures, the storage account container becomes accessible via Azure File Explorer.
You can set up lures for container registry decoys using browser lures, file decoys, and session lures.
You can use browser lures or session lures to configure lures for VM image decoys.

lure-key-vault-vmimage.statement: A key vault decoy's lures use file decoys or session lures, and its enumeration and subsequent interaction with other decoy resources are logged as attacks; a VM image decoy logs an attack when an adversary boots it to launch an instance and it communicates with Deception.

quotes: You can configure lures for key vault decoys using file decoys or session lures.
The enumeration of key vault decoys and subsequent interaction with other decoy resources are logged as attacks.
When an adversary uses the VM image decoy and boots it up to launch an instance, the VM image decoy communicates with Zscaler Deception and logs the event as an attack.

lure-page-copy-text.statement: The Azure lures page's storage account file share entry and container registry entry each say "An interaction with the storage account container decoy is logged as an attack.", and the VM image decoy entry is followed by the link line "To learn more about container registries, refer to the Microsoft documentation.".

quotes: An interaction with the storage account container decoy is logged as an attack.
evidence.after: The file share decoys are mounted on endpoints using cloud lures or session lures.

quotes: An interaction with the storage account container decoy is logged as an attack.
evidence.after: You can set up lures for container registry decoys using browser lures, file decoys, and session lures.

quotes: To learn more about container registries, refer to the Microsoft documentation.
evidence.after: the VM image decoy communicates with Zscaler Deception and logs the event as an attack.

delete-abort.statement: During Azure account deletion in Cloud Shell, entering n at the continue-with-deletion prompt aborts the deletion and the configuration is enabled again in the Admin Portal; Admin Portal deletion disables the configuration.

quotes: If you enter n and press Enter, then the deletion process is aborted, and the configuration is enabled again in the Deception Admin Portal.
All fields are deleted, and the configuration is disabled in the Deception Admin Portal.

resource-group-delete.statement: Resource groups created by Deception are listed on the Resource Group Management tab and can be deleted there; if the group was not yet created in Azure (No in the Created column) deletion completes in the portal, otherwise the admin signs in to the Azure Portal as a Cloud Device Administrator or Global Administrator and runs the deployment script in Cloud Shell, entering the option to sync settings.

quotes: The list of all resource groups created by Zscaler Deception in the Microsoft Azure portal is displayed on the Resource Group Management tab (Deceive > Cloud Deception).
If the deleted resource group was not already created in the Azure portal (indicated by No in the Created column), the deletion is complete and you can skip the following steps.
Sign in to the Azure Portal as a Cloud Device Administrator or Global Administrator.
Run the deployment script using the command obtained via the automated download method or manual download method.
Enter the option to sync settings and press Enter.

azure-admin-roles.summary: The Azure setup page requires a user with Cloud Device Administrator and Global Administrator roles to run the deployment script; the user decoy page and the resource group page have the admin sign in as a Cloud Device Administrator or Global Administrator.

quotes: An Azure user with Cloud Device Administrator and Global Administrator roles to run the deployment script.

positions.says: The user running the deployment script needs the Cloud Device Administrator and Global Administrator roles.

quotes: Sign in to the Azure Portal as a Cloud Device Administrator or Global Administrator.

positions.says: The user decoy page has the admin sign in to the Azure Portal as a Cloud Device Administrator or Global Administrator.

azure-admin-roles.impact: Whether the deployment script needs both roles or either one is not settled by the pages.

azure-health-check-meaning.summary: The Azure integration page says the health check function app monitors and updates the health status of the deployed decoys; the deployment-script page says the function app does not check the actual health of the deployed Azure resources.

quotes: A health check function app is also deployed that monitors and updates the health status of the deployed decoys to the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal every 15 minutes.

positions.says: The health check function app monitors and updates the health status of the deployed decoys every 15 minutes.

quotes: This function app does not check the actual health of the deployed Azure resources.

positions.says: The function app does not check the actual health of the deployed Azure resources.

azure-health-check-meaning.impact: Whether a healthy status in the Admin Portal reflects the health of the Azure resources, or only that they exist, is not settled by the pages.

arm-history-event.title: Whether the ARM template deployment-history entry itself alerts
arm-history-event.detail: The lures page says ARM template decoys do not generate an event, while the identities they embed can be used by an adversary. No captured page says whether reading the deployment-history entry itself ever produces an alert.
